To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the natural history and screening characteristics of cancers in BRCA mutation carriers are different for BRCA1 compared to BRCA2, and the benefits of screening are similar in both groups.

the natural history of breast cancers in BRCA mutation carriers differs substantially between BRCA1 and between BRCA2 mutation, with BRCA2 cancers presenting later and being smaller and less aggressive.

the natural history and screening outcomes of breast cancer in BRCA1/ BRCA2 mutation carrier women differ, that MRI screening is highly sensitive in detecting breast cancer, and that the use of combined MRI and mammography screening is associated with a significant reduction in breast cancer mortality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new and improved methods for the detection of breast cancer in high-risk women, and the use of such methods in the development of new screening protocols.
the natural history of BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 mutation-associated breast cancer, and the role of breast cancer screening with MRI and mammography in the prevention of breast cancer mortality.
understanding the natural history of breast cancers in BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 carriers, and the effectiveness of breast cancer screening.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no clear benefit to using MRI in BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation carrier women under the age of 30 years, and the benefit of using MRI for women aged 40 years and above is unclear.

the evidence from the MRISC, MARIB, and MARH study is insufficient to determine whether MRI screening of women at risk for breast cancer due to a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation reduces breast cancer–specific mortality or all-cause mortality.

the use of annual screening MRI in BRCA1/ BRCA2 mutation carries reduces breast cancer deaths by 50% to more than 60%, but that there may be a need to modify the screening strategy for women with a BRCA1 mutation, for example, by reducing the screening interval to every 6 months below the age of about 40 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BRCA1 and BCRA2 carriers have very different breast cancer risks and different natural history.
we have shown that there are important differences in the biology of breast cancers in BRCA mutation carriers and that these differences are important in the development of screening protocols.

the differences in natural history of breast cancers between BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers are important and that the use of MRI for screening in these mutation carriers is beneficial, but that the differences in screening performance between BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation carrier cohorts are likely due to differences in the natural histories between BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, rather than to differences in the screening performance of mammography or MRI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BRCA1 mutation and BRCA2 carriers have very different breast cancers, and they may need to be managed differently.
BRCA1 andBRCA2 mutation carriers are at high risk for breast cancer, and that MRI can detect breast cancers at an early stage, when they are still small.
there are substantial clinical differences in natural histories between BRCA1 andBRCA2 mutation carriers.
